articles.title_orig: Nvidia board probes Jensen Huang China spy allegations
articles.title_zh: Nvidia board probes Jensen Huang China spy allegations
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia’s board has launched an independent investigation into allegations that its chief executive officer, Jensen Huang, was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation involving a woman suspected of working for China’s intelligence service.
The company announced the investigation on Nov. 8, following reports that U.S. intelligence officials believed Alice Huang, an executive associated with Singapore-based technology company Megaspeed International, had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security. This was to gather information about the Nvidia chief and the semiconductor industry.
The investigation will be overseen by an independent committee of Nvidia directors, assisted by external legal counsel. The company’s board said it had no reason to believe that U.S. national security or Nvidia’s confidential information had been compromised.
“Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it,” the board said in its statement, adding that it had confidence in Huang and the company’s leadership team.
The announcement followed a report by The New York Times, cited by Bloomberg on Nov. 6. U.S. intelligence officials believed Alice Huang had been recruited by Chinese intelligence to collect information on Jensen Huang and potentially influence Nvidia’s business decisions.
According to an Axios report on Nov. 8, Jensen Huang acknowledged having a romantic relationship with the woman in a draft email to Nvidia employees. In the message, he apologized to his family and colleagues, saying, “I owe my family and all of you an apology.”
READ: Trump administration cancels tech panel meeting including Nvidia, Meta CEOs (November 6, 2026)
Nvidia’s public policy communications chief, John Rizzo, said the developments would not disrupt the company’s operations and that Huang remained committed to continuing as CEO without interruption.
The allegations have drawn attention because of Nvidia’s central role in the global artificial intelligence industry and the strategic importance of its advanced chips in the U.S.-China technology competition.
Alice Huang was associated with Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based company that purchases Nvidia’s artificial intelligence processors. The company has come under U.S. scrutiny over allegations that advanced Nvidia chips were being diverted to Chinese customers in violation of American export restrictions.
U.S. intelligence officials reportedly believed that Alice Huang had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to obtain information about American AI technology and potentially influence Nvidia to make its most advanced processors available to Chinese customers.
The allegations also raise questions about the access business executives and intermediaries can obtain to sensitive technology companies and their leadership.
Nvidia has previously defended its business relationship with Megaspeed. In an October 29 interview with Bloomberg, Huang described the company’s dealings with the Singapore-based firm as “normal and not unusual.”
He said Nvidia had examined Megaspeed’s GPU deployments to ensure that its processors were not being illegally diverted to China. Huang also described his interactions with the company’s executives as typical of his engagements with customers in the region.
Nvidia has maintained that its regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information rather than sensitive company trade secrets or information relevant to U.S. national security.
Huang, 63, co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has served as its president and chief executive officer since the company’s establishment. His 33-year tenure makes him one of the longest-serving chief executives in the American technology industry.
Born in Tainan, Taiwan, on Feb. 17, 1963, Huang moved to the United States as a child. He attended Oregon State University, where he earned a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering, before completing a master’s degree in electrical engineering at Stanford University.
Before establishing Nvidia with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, Huang worked at semiconductor companies Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) and LSI Logic.
He worked as a microprocessor designer at AMD before joining LSI Logic in 1985, where he held engineering and leadership positions. He remained there until 1993, when he co-founded Nvidia with his two partners.
READ: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang joins Trump on his China visit (May 13, 2026)
Under Huang’s leadership, Nvidia evolved from a graphics processing unit manufacturer serving the computer gaming industry into one of the world’s most influential semiconductor companies. Its GPUs have become central to the development and operation of artificial intelligence systems, large data centers and advanced computing infrastructure.
Huang’s birthplace and family background have also drawn attention amid the allegations involving Chinese intelligence. Although born in Taiwan, Huang moved to the United States during childhood and built his career in the American technology industry. Taiwan is self-governed and has a separate political and administrative system from mainland China.
His Taiwanese heritage should not be confused with an association with the Chinese government. There is no evidence in the reports that Huang himself was involved in any Chinese intelligence operation.
His professional engagement with China, however, has been an important part of Nvidia’s business and the wider debate over American restrictions on advanced semiconductor exports.
Huang has repeatedly advocated allowing Nvidia to compete in the Chinese market, arguing that restricting American technology companies could create opportunities for competitors. Washington has imposed export controls on advanced AI processors to limit China’s access to technology considered strategically important to national security.
The latest investigation comes as Nvidia faces increased scrutiny over its international customer relationships, chip distribution and the potential diversion of advanced processors to China. Nvidia’s board has not announced a conclusion from its investigation. The allegations involving Alice Huang and any possible transfer of confidential information remain subject to examination.
Johnson Myalil is an immigration attorney at the Washington, DC,-based High-Tech Immigration Law Group. He earned his Juris Doctor degree from Valparaiso University in Indiana and an LL.M. degree from The George Washington University in Washington, DC. Myalil specializes in employment-based immigration.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia launches investigation into CEO's affair with suspected Chinese spy
articles.title_zh: Nvidia launches investigation into CEO's affair with suspected Chinese spy
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia has opened an investigation into co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a businesswoman who intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy.
U.S. intelligence agencies have expressed concerns that the woman, Alice Huang, who is affiliated with a cloud company and an Nvidia customer called Megaspeed, has been passing information to Beijing, according to reports in The New York Times and the Financial Times.
Huang told Nvidia staff in an email on Sunday that he had an affair with the woman and that Nvidia's board of directors had opened an independent investigation into the spying allegations.
"I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did," Huang wrote in the message. "I am deeply sorry."
An Nvidia spokesperson said that Huang was committed to continuing as CEO of Nvidia without interruption.
In a statement, the Nvidia board said it would investigate the allegations that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.
"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," Nvidia's board said in a statement.
The allegations come as Nvidia has become the center of a trade dispute between China and the U.S. as AI is seen as increasingly critical to national security.
The U.S. restricts exports of Nvidia's most advanced AI chips to China, though it has approved exports of certain older, slower models.
Megaspeed, which Alice Huang is affiliated with, has been accused of helping restricted Chinese companies acquire Nvidia AI chips. Nvidia representatives previously said that Megaspeed had already been investigated for evading export controls.
Nvidia's Huang has pushed for broader AI chip exports to China, saying it is better for the U.S. if the world uses and builds on American technology. He has also aligned with President Donald Trump on American artificial intelligence policy and its infrastructure buildout.
In his note to staff, Huang said he was "proud and grateful" to be an American.
Three House Republican committee chairs sent a letter to Huang on Wednesday asking him to sit for a closed-door briefing with lawmakers on Nov. 18.
Nvidia reports third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17 and will hold a major conference in Washington, D.C., at the end of the month.

articles.title_orig: Cruise ship pianist rescued after nine hours treading water miles from shore
articles.title_zh: Cruise ship pianist rescued after nine hours treading water miles from shore
articles.content_orig:
Man taken to hospital after falling off Royal Caribbean ship in Pacific Ocean, with Coast Guard investigating incident
A pianist for a Royal Caribbean cruise ship is expected to survive after two Newport Beach, California , fishermen discovered him treading water in the Pacific Ocean nearly 20 miles (32km) offshore on Friday.
The unidentified man was taken to the hospital after the rescue, according to the US Coast Guard, which is now investigating how he went overboard from the cruise ship.
Authorities believe the man may have been in the ocean for approximately nine hours before he was spotted by Sean Norton and Grant Garrett, who were returning from a fishing trip near Catalina Island.
The two fishermen had spent the morning fishing for marlin when their trip took an unexpected turn. By noon, they had pulled the stranded man from the water.
“I’m like, ‘Yeah, it’s a human being. Stop the boat; let’s get all of our lines in,” Garrett told CBS News , recalling the moment the boat’s captain first saw the man in the water.
The fishermen quickly worked together to bring the man onboard. Once the man regained his composure, Garrett said he identified himself as a pianist onboard Royal Caribbean’s 14-deck cruise ship, the “Ovation of the Seas.”
According to Norton, the rescued crew member had few words to describe what he had just experienced. “The only thing he said to me was, ‘Thank you. I thought I was gonna die,’” Norton said.
After the rescue, the fishing crew issued an emergency maritime call, prompting Newport Beach lifeguards to respond and provide assistance. Battalion chief Adam Yacenda said the man was found approximately 15 to 20 miles offshore, according to CBS, or “pretty much in the middle of the ocean”.
Despite the extended time spent in the water, Norton believes unusually warm ocean temperatures may have played a significant role in the man’s survival.
“You have this crazy super El Niño year. This guy was in the water for probably 10 hours, but the water’s 76 degrees,” Norton said. “A different year, no way he makes it.”
The circumstances surrounding the crew member’s fall from the cruise ship remain under investigation by the Coast Guard. Royal Caribbean Group acknowledged the incident and said it is assisting the employee following the ordeal.
In a statement to CBS, a company spokesperson said: “We are providing support and assistance to our crew member during this difficult time. To respect the privacy of our employee, we have no additional details to share.”

articles.title_orig: Collision between 2 trains in Egypt kills 7 and injures at least 125
articles.title_zh: Collision between 2 trains in Egypt kills 7 and injures at least 125
articles.content_orig:
President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 30 miles from Cairo
Seven people were killed and more than 100 injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, officials said.
The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 30 miles south of Cairo, when a train travelling to Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry.
An inspection indicated that the Cairo-Aswan train had been stationary on the same track, officials said.
Train derailments and crashes are common in Egypt, where the railway system has a history of mismanagement and poor maintenance of equipment. In recent years the government has announced modernisation initiatives to improve its railways.
Ayman Gamal, a resident of Kafr Girza in al-Ayyat where the crash occurred, said people rushed to the scene, pulled out survivors and called ambulances.
Gamal said he saw about 80 of the injured being taken by ambulances to hospital. He said some passengers were trapped inside one of the carriages of the stationary train and died.
Egypt’s president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, said in a social media post that he had ordered a prompt investigation.
Emergency teams and cranes were dispatched to the scene to clear the wreckage and restore train services to their normal schedule as soon as possible, the Egyptian railway authority said.
Last September, a train driver and his assistant were injured after two freight trains collided in the same district.
Egypt’s deadliest train crash was in 2002 when more than 300 people were killed after a fire broke out on an overnight train journeying from Cairo to southern Egypt.

articles.title_orig: UN agency for Palestinian refugees eyeing major restructuring
articles.title_zh: UN agency for Palestinian refugees eyeing major restructuring
articles.content_orig:
The United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA) is considering a major restructuring that could see thousands of its employees laid off and some of its responsibilities transferred to other bodies, including US President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace, according to multiple media reports citing diplomatic sources.
The reported proposal is spearheaded by UNRWA’s acting commissioner-general, Christian Saunders, and comes as the agency faces a severe financial crisis.
Trump’s Board of Peace (BoP), established under the framework endorsed by the UN Security Council in November 2025, is tasked with overseeing Gaza’s transitional governance, reconstruction, economic recovery, and coordination of humanitarian assistance.
The BoP has been explicit in its opposition to the UN agency set up for Palestinian refugees only, making it clear in a July 1 statement that “UNRWA has no place in the new Gaza .”
“We are turning the page on the complex of perpetual aid dependency and conflict. The people of Gaza deserve better,” the BoP said in a social media post on September 25.
In the same post, the BoP said it would “only work with trusted partners who will deliver for the people of Gaza and contribute to a de-radicalized Strip. UNRWA fails on those litmus tests.”
However, the Associated Press reported, also on September 25, that BoP representatives have held several private meetings with UNRWA officials. A BoP official acknowledged that some of the agency’s programs and vetted employees could continue if they were effective and accountable, while maintaining that the UN body’s institutional role was ending.
UN Watch’s Hillel Neuer posted last week that there is a plan to unravel UNRWA, which has long faced criticism from Israel, the United States, and UN Watch over allegations of links between some of its employees and terrorist organizations such as Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad (PIJ) – including participating in October 7 and holding hostages.
According to Israel Hayom , which cited Arab and Western diplomatic sources, discussions have taken place about transferring some of UNRWA’s responsibilities to the BoP and other bodies.
Some of the agency’s remit could reportedly also be transferred to the Palestinian Authority (PA) in the West Bank.
The reported proposal was presented by Saunders at a meeting of UNRWA’s Advisory Commission, with the agency’s financial difficulties cited as a central reason for the restructuring. Saunders told Anadolu Agency on October 20 that the agency’s deficit stood at approximately $70 million.
“If we don’t receive money in the very near future, I will have to take some regrettable actions in order to ensure that we’re able to finish the year and to pay our staff salaries,” Saunders warned.
The head of the Arab Staff Union in Gaza, Mustafa Al-Ghoul, told the Mondoweiss anti-Zionist news site last week that UNRWA had dismissed around 1,000 staff in Gaza and let 2,000 retire without replacing them, leaving roughly 10,500.
Saunders gave the same figures in the Anadolu Agency interview, saying “We have 10,500 personnel on the ground [in the Gaza Strip].”
He also expressed support for the broader international framework for Gaza, saying: “ US President Trump ’s 20-point plan, UN Security Council Resolution 2803, the Board of Peace, and the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza – we are completely behind these efforts.”
Separately, Swiss French-language daily newspaper Le Temps published an investigation last week saying that Saunders plans for UNRWA to close its doors “within four or five years.” This has not yet been independently verified.
Under the UN-backed framework, the BoP is to exercise transitional authority in Gaza until the PA has completed its reform program and can securely and effectively resume control. In the meantime, the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza is intended to serve as an interim technocratic administration.
Currently, UNRWA purports to be assisting more than 1.7 million Palestinians in Gaza, providing healthcare through 11 centers, schooling for approximately 300,000 children, and drinking water for around 820,000 people.
It also says it provides essential services to nearly six million Palestinian refugees across Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, and the West Bank.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been asked by three House Republican  committee chairs to brief Congress behind closed doors about his reported ties to a woman accused of spying for China.

articles.title_orig: China's half-price Rolls-Royce: Yangwang Altior is a lavish alternative to a Phantom limo
articles.title_zh: China's half-price Rolls-Royce: Yangwang Altior is a lavish alternative to a Phantom limo
articles.content_orig:
By ROB HULL, MOTORING EDITOR
Updated: 13:34 EDT, 8 November 2026
We've had the Temu Range Rover; now there's an AliExpress Roller.
Chinese brand Yangwang, a spin-off from electric car giant BYD, has unveiled a new battery-powered luxury vehicle called the Altior, and it bears a striking resemblance to the iconic British Rolls-Royce Phantom limousine – but for around half the price.
At 5.6m long, with a vast bonnet and grille, rear-hinged coach doors, a palatial interior and umbrellas stowed inside the door panels, there's no hiding which ostentatious motor it has firmly set its sights on.
Altior means 'higher' in Latin, with the car 'expressing an ambition to elevate the experience of luxury through cultural depth, personal expression and technological progress', Yangwang says.
Just 399 are going to be produced and reports in China suggest pre-orders are available from 2million yuan, which equates to around £230,000.
That puts it closer to the £250,000 Rolls-Royce Ghost than the flagship £450,000 Phantom, though that's before taking into account heavily subsidised pricing in China's domestic market.
Its global premiere in Abu Dhabi this weekend comes just days after car registration figures revealed that Jaecoo's 'Temu Range Rover' 7 SUV was the UK's best-selling new model for a second successive month .
The runaway success of the Range Rover Velar lookalike is the clearest sign yet that Chinese brands are coming for the old guard of established luxury carmakers. And with the Altior, it appears not even Rolls-Royce is safe.
This is the new Yangwang Altior limousine - a luxury Rolls-Royce Phantom rival from Chinese EV giant, BYD
While the Rolls-Royce Phantom and Ghost feature a gutsy 6.75-litre twin-turbocharged V12 petrol engine, the Yangwang Altior is a far greener proposition.
It uses a version of the quad-electric motor setup deployed in the Chinese firm's other models, the U8 SUV and U9 supercar. That's likely to produce more than 1,000bhp and will allow it to perform a tank turn , rotating each wheel independently to spin the vehicle on its own axis.
Providing the energy for the e-motors is BYD's second-generation Blade Battery technology.
As such, it's claimed to be capable of travelling more than 621 miles on a full charge. However, this is based on Chinese efficiency tests that are historically a shade more optimistic than Europe's cycle, which would be closer to 520 miles.
The battery is compatible with BYD's network of Flash Charging stations, of which there are 10,000 already in China and a promise to install 300 here in the UK .
The ground-breaking devices can deliver up to 1,500kW of power and top up a battery pack from 10 to 70 per cent charge in as little as five minutes, before reaching full charge in less than ten.
That's not all in terms of technological advances.
The Yangwang boasts a suite of chassis tech that means it can float if there are flash floods or the driver 'accidentally enters water'. And it can continue tracking in a straight line when one of the tyres suffers a high-speed blowout on the motorway.
The Altior also taps into BYD's God's Eye A assisted-driving system, which includes parking-space-to-parking-space navigation assistance. This enables the car to drive itself from one car park to another, even when they are hundreds of miles apart.
The suspension is clever too. The brand's DiSus active body control system uses cameras to read the road ahead and adjusts damping in real time, meaning occupants won't feel potholes or changes in road surfaces while stretched out in the back.
Altior means 'higher' in Latin, as BYD's spin-off Yangwang looks to enter a more opulent market with its latest model. And it certain strikes a resemblance to the Rolls-Royce Phantom
Squint slightly and there's no mistaking the Rolls-Royce-inspired silhouette.
The elongated bonnet, despite there being no 12-cylinder combustion engine lurking beneath it, and the glitzy upright grille are trademarks of the 122-year-old British marque.
The Altior's front end is described as a 'masterpiece of high jewellery'.
'Meticulous selection, polishing and individual placement create a composition that responds to changing light, revealing new depth and brilliance as the viewpoint moves,' the Chinese manufacturer says.
Its lights are a little special too, featuring 12 individual elements that rotate from the outside to the centre to create a 'ceremonial welcome' when the owner approaches.
At 5.6m long, the Altior (pictured left) is 5.5cm longer than the Ghost and 16cm shorter than the Phantom (pictured right)
Like all Roller limousines, the Chinese Yangwang has rear-hinged coach doors
Twenty-one-inch wheels are standard, with the dish-style monoblock design bearing more than a passing resemblance to the disc rims available on a Phantom
Is it time for European luxury car makers to fear China’s fast-rising electric rivals?
At 5.6m long, the Altior is 5.5cm longer than the Ghost and 16cm shorter than the Phantom.
However, the Yangwang's other dimensions, including a width of 2m, a height of almost 1.6m and a wheelbase of 3.5m, are almost like-for-like with the bigger of the two Rolls-Royces.
Twenty-one-inch wheels are standard, with the dish-style monoblock design bearing more than a passing resemblance to the disc rims available on a Phantom.
The doors also open in the fashion for which Rolls-Royce is famed, providing generous access to the opulent interior.
The finely crafted bespoke umbrellas hidden in each door panel, much like those in a Rolls-Royce, are said to be inspired by the circular wooden roof of the Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests at China's Temple of Heaven complex.
The cockpit is the least Roller-like part of the car. While the British luxury firm attempts to conceal tech for a traditional look, the Yangwang has a dashboard-wide high-definition screen
Exactly like Rolls-Royces, though, the Chinese limo has bespoke, hand-crafted umbrellas hidden in a compartment within the doors
Step inside and the cabin – dubbed a 'private lounge' – is awash with only the highest-quality materials.
These include hammer-tested metal switches, pure-wool floor mats, real-wood veneers, 48 jewellery-inspired control buttons and semi-aniline leather upholstery.
The designers have even mounted polished yellow jade gemstones inside the vertical air vents, while the silk-embroidered door panels feature cloud and thunder-pattern motifs.
The cockpit itself looks a little less Rolls-Royce-esque, even if it does feature a chrome-rimmed steering wheel wrapped in beautifully finished leather.
While the British car maker generally tries to subtly conceal much of its modern technology up front, the Yangwang has a dashboard-spanning digital glass display. This incorporates an instrument cluster with classic-style digital dials and an enormous infotainment screen featuring a laptop-style taskbar of icons.
But it's the rear compartment that well-heeled customers will want to know about.
The cabin is as palatial as you'd expect from a Rolls-Royce or Bentley limo. It boasts aviation-style zero-gravity seats, real-wood veneers and 48 jewellery-inspired control buttons
There's a fridge in the rear and in the front, two champagne flute holders and a control panel that means you won't have to converse with your chauffeur at all
There's plenty of artistry too. Silk-embroidered door panels feature cloud and thunder-pattern motifs
The four-seat layout is almost perfectly symmetrical and 'gives each occupant a clearly defined personal space' where the owner in the back can feel entirely separate from Jeeves behind the wheel by elevating a divider between them.
Owners won't need to ask their chauffeur for anything, either.
Rear occupants can access all key functions through the central console, including lowering the front passenger seat at the touch of a button to provide an uninterrupted view ahead.

articles.title_orig: Trump unveils 'Iron Gate' task force against Iran as Saudis launch deadly strikes on Houthi rebels
articles.title_zh: Trump unveils 'Iron Gate' task force against Iran as Saudis launch deadly strikes on Houthi rebels
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump said Sunday that a renewed war with Iran is “highly unlikely” if Tehran makes progress toward a nuclear agreement and reopens the Strait of Hormuz — while warning that the U.S. has 38 Iranian bridges in its sights.
“It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement,” Trump told CNN .
Trump said military action would probably not be necessary, but warned that the U.S. is prepared to strike Iran again.
“The answer is highly unlikely it’s going to be necessary,” Trump said. “They’re a failing nation. It just came out, you saw this year, 301% inflation. Highly unlikely it will be necessary. I would if necessary, but we hit them really hard. I hit them so hard. You don’t know how hard I hit them.”
Trump added that it is “highly unlikely” he would have to order another attack.
“They’re withering away financially. We’ve hit them militarily. We could finish them off,” he warned.
“We’re ready for it. I’ve got three aircraft carriers here. The other one just arrived. We have three. They’re fully locked and loaded,” Trump continued.
He also said the U.S. could destroy dozens of bridges in Iran within hours.
“We have 38 bridges in our sight that we can knock down in literally one hour,” Trump said. “They’ll all be down.”
“I don’t want to do that because, essentially, it’ll take 10 years to rebuild them,” he added. “I don’t like ripping down bridges. And the hardest thing to build is a bridge. It takes years, and I’m a good builder.”
Diplomatic activity across the Middle East has continued since Thursday, with Qatar mediating efforts to advance talks between Washington and Tehran
President Donald Trump on Sunday touted Washington’s new U.S. military task force aimed at choking off Iran's weapons supply routes, as it ramps up pressure through its maritime blockade.
“Task Force Iron Gate is in full force and effect in the Islamic Republic of Iran ,” Trump said on Truth Social.
“Coupled with history’s greatest Naval Blockade, very little gets into, or out of, Iran!” he added.
U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) announced the formation of Task Force Iron Gate on Saturday, saying the roughly 20-person team will be based in Tampa, Florida, and work to disrupt the movement of weapons, sanctioned materials and illicit revenue across Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea.
The U.S. Treasury Department asked that Iraq shut down all but two of its border crossings with Iran as part of a drive to isolate Tehran, Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said Sunday, according to Reuters .
“There are many official and unofficial border crossings with Iran, and closing all of them would be difficult and would affect our economy.
“The Americans are still demanding the closure of the crossings, and we are currently in discussions with them,” Hussein said in an interview with Al Jazeera.
The development came as U.S. Central Command ( CENTCOM ) moved to close off Tehran’s overland corridors militarily, directing the establishment of Task Force Iron Gate on Nov. 7.
Adm. Brad Cooper said the initiative was to build on the “success of our ironclad blockade against Iran at sea” and would “further constrain Iran’s ability to finance terrorism, rebuild weapons factories, and replenish their military.”
Iran's foreign minister issued a stark ultimatum to the White House on Sunday, warning that Tehran's forces would "rain down hell" if Washington chooses war over a diplomatic proposal aimed at ending the war.
“American voters have made their choice. Time for the White House to make its own,” Abbas Araghchi said of the latest proposal sent to Washington.
“Our 2-day proposal stands: meet the requirements, including end to war on all fronts, and you will see results,” he said on X .
“Or choose war, and see our alert and battle-hardened Warriors rain down hell,” he warned.
According to Reuters , Araghchi also said Sunday that the midterm results had temporarily stalled mediation efforts aimed at securing a deal between Tehran and Washington.
Araghchi told Iranian state television that Tehran would have to wait for mediators to resume diplomatic efforts.

articles.title_orig: King leads solemn Remembrance Sunday service at Cenotaph
articles.title_zh: King leads solemn Remembrance Sunday service at Cenotaph
articles.content_orig:
King Charles III led the nation in a solemn two-minute silence on Remembrance Sunday in London to honour veterans who had died in conflict.
On a stone-grey autumn morning, he laid a wreath at the Cenotaph in Whitehall before a march-past by 10,000 armed forces veterans.
That included a shrinking number of World War Two veterans, with 12 taking part this year, including 103-year-old Annie Duplock, who described it as a "very emotional day".
Meanwhile, the number of former prime ministers reached a record high, with nine lined up to lay wreaths, while Andy Burnham attended for the first time as the current occupant of No 10 Downing Street.
And for the first time, the leader of Reform UK, Nigel Farage, had enough MPs in Parliament to qualify to lay a wreath alongside other major party leaders.
The Prince of Wales and the Princess Royal were among royals in attendance, along with military chiefs, senior politicians, diplomats and faith leaders, watched by big crowds squeezed behind railings along Whitehall.
Queen Camilla and the Princess of Wales watched from a balcony above the Cenotaph in the Foreign Office.
Among the flags on the roof of that Whitehall building was the Ukrainian blue and yellow. It went up when Russia invaded and four years later it is now visibly frayed - a reminder of the length of that war and of current threats.
At 11:00 GMT, as the first strike of Big Ben echoed from the nearby Houses of Parliament, the big two-minute silence filled the usually frenetic streets, before the playing of the Last Post.
The King had his eyes closed, the crowds in Whitehall stopped for their own thoughts, in a rare moment of calm in the capital.
The poignant parade past the Cenotaph included representatives of about 340 different military and civilian groups, from the Royal Naval Association and the Royal Marines Association to Transport for London and the Royal National Lifeboat Institute.
Alongside those marching were flotillas of disability scooters and families helping veterans in wheelchairs.
Those who took part in WW2 are now increasingly frail - and there were 12 participants in the march-past compared to 20 last year. The oldest participant this year was aged 105.
Taking part for the first time was 103-year-old Annie Duplock, who had been part of the Land Army that had helped to feed the country at war.
She had joined the Land Army in 1940 as a 16-year-old, having lied about her age, and worked on a farm in Leicestershire.
"I feel very honoured to be taking part in the parade and to represent the Land Girls. I'm very excited, although a little apprehensive as I don't quite know what to expect," she said.
"I think it will be a very emotional day, bringing back memories of all those who didn't return home. It will be lovely to be there and remember them."
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the annual event was a time to "reflect on the selflessness and courage it takes to commit your life to protecting others".
He earlier announced that he wanted to tackle the problem of homelessness among ex-service personnel to "ensure that any veteran sleeping rough is offered appropriate accommodation before Christmas".
Mark Atkinson, the director general of the Royal British Legion, said: "As we come together on Remembrance Sunday, we pay tribute to all those who have served and sacrificed, from generations past to those still serving today."
Remembrance events took place across the country as thousands gathered to pay their respects to those who died in past conflicts.
First Minister of Scotland John Swinney placed a wreath at the Stone of Remembrance outside the City Chambers during an event in Edinburgh.
Veterans, military personnel and cadets also marched through the centres of British cities such as Manchester, Birmingham and Leeds.
A silent poppy drop was held as part of the Festival of Remembrance at Durham Cathedral while wreaths were laid at Canterbury Cathedral.
Separately, the Duke of Sussex was seen attending a Remembrance service in the market town of Brackley in Northamptonshire.
For more than a century, the national Remembrance event has been held around the Cenotaph.
The monument was built as a focal point for honouring those who had fought and died in World War One, including those who had no grave, and as a place to mourn for those families who might not be able to visit war cemeteries overseas.
The word "cenotaph" means "empty tomb" in Greek and it was designed by the architect Sir Edwin Lutyens in a simple, austere style, with no sense of triumphalism and with almost no decoration.
The monument had been originally built in 1919 as a temporary, plaster and wood structure. But it proved so popular with the public that it was replaced in 1920 with a permanent version, in the same design but in stone.
It was opened at 11:00 on 11 November 1920 by King George V. His great-grandson, Charles, was there again, on an overcast morning 106 years later, to continue paying respect.

articles.title_orig: Eisenkot open to Netanyahu joining Israel’s next government
articles.title_zh: Eisenkot open to Netanyahu joining Israel’s next government
articles.content_orig:
Israel’s opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot , the man officially tasked by President Isaac Herzog with trying to form the country’s next government, has said that he was open to including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in his coalition lineup.
In a speech at Sunday’s ceremony in Herzog’s office in Jerusalem, Eisenkot suggested Netanyahu’s far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich was also welcome to join.
“If members of Likud and the Religious Zionist Party truly believe this is a time for unity, as they told the president, I cannot conceive of any reason why they would not support a government under my leadership and the principles I have presented,” Eisenkot said.
Eisenkot, who ran as Netanyahu’s main rival, has six weeks to form a new government. At the ceremony, Eisenkot said he will act in the interests of the public and represent all parts of Israeli society.
Herzog, meanwhile, warned that the country faced uncertainties after the November 3 midterm elections in the United States, which brought victories for several political figures critical of Israel and the US’s military support.
“The State of Israel needs a stable government,” Herzog said, pointing to the “new political reality” in the US.
Eisenkot led Israel’s military from 2015 to 2019 and sat as an observer in Netanyahu’s war cabinet for the first eight months of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, which began in October 2023.
Despite this, Arab-led parties endorsed Eisenkot for the mandate to replace Netanyahu.
In Israel’s October 27 elections , Eisenkot’s four-party alliance won 48 seats, while Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious bloc secured 53, leaving both short of the 61 needed for a parliamentary majority. Arab-led parties, representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, won a record 19 seats.
Eisenkot has ruled out forming a government with the Arab-led parties, which would give him a 67-seat bloc. Winning over the two ultra-Orthodox parties, United Torah Judaism and Shas, would give him exactly 61 seats.
He could also form a government with fewer than 61 seats if he wins a parliamentary confidence vote.
“Netanyahu still has time to derail Gadi Eisenkot’s efforts to form a government and sabotage attempts to gain a vote of confidence,” said Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from Ramallah, in the occupied West Bank.
“In the meantime, he remains caretaker prime minister. If Eisenkot fails, Netanyahu would be the natural second in line to be tasked with forming a government. And if he fails, elections would then be called, and that would still allow Netanyahu to remain as caretaker.
“Many of Netanyahu’s critics say that is his aim. The big question in Israeli politics now is: does the opposition really want to get rid of Netanyahu? Or is the opposition to Palestinian Israelis in mainstream politics so strong that they’re willing to risk keeping Netanyahu in power by going back to the ballot box?”

articles.title_orig: A Missionary Pope Faces a Chain Saw-Wielding Populist in Argentina
articles.title_zh: A Missionary Pope Faces a Chain Saw-Wielding Populist in Argentina
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV arrived in Argentina in the afternoon of Sunday, 8 November, for the second leg of his 12-day apostolic journey to three South American nations, following his visit to Uruguay. The journey will conclude in Peru.
The papal aircraft, an Aerolíneas Argentinas Boeing 737 MAX, covered the 365-kilometre journey from Montevideo to Buenos Aires in approximately one hour, flying over Uruguay and Argentina.
The Pope landed at Aeroparque Jorge Newbery International Airport in Buenos Aires, where an official welcome ceremony took place in the airport's military area.
Upon the aircraft's arrival, Apostolic Nuncio to Argentina Archbishop Michael Wallace Banach and the Argentinian Chief of Protocol boarded the plane to greet the Pope.
Argentinian President Javier Milei then welcomed Pope Leo XIV at the foot of the aircraft's stairs.
The official ceremony included military honours, the national anthems of the Holy See and Argentina, and a floral offering presented by two children. The respective delegations were also introduced.
Archbishop Banach, who was appointed Apostolic Nuncio to Argentina on 14 May 2026, and Archbishop Marcelo Daniel Colombo of Mendoza, President of the Argentinian Episcopal Conference, are among the Church representatives accompanying the Pope's visit.
The visit carries particular significance given Buenos Aires' close connection with Pope Francis, who served as Archbishop of the Argentine capital from 28 February 1998 until his election as Pope on 13 March 2013.
Buenos Aires, Argentina's capital and most populous city, is situated on the western bank of the Río de la Plata. It is one of the major political, cultural and financial centres of Latin America and has long been a focal point of the country's social and economic life.
Founded in 1536 by Spanish conquistador Pedro de Mendoza and re-established in 1580 by Juan de Garay, the city became the capital of the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata in 1776. It played a central role in Argentina's struggle for independence, which began with the May Revolution of 1810.
Today, Buenos Aires is divided into 15 communes and 48 neighbourhoods, known as barrios . Its history has also been shaped by successive waves of immigration, particularly from Europe during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.
Following the official welcome and meeting with the Argentinian President, Pope Leo XIV is scheduled to travel by car to Plaza San Martín, just over 6 kilometres from the airport.
Located in the Retiro neighbourhood, the historic square is named after General José de San Martín, one of the principal leaders of South America's independence movements and a national hero in Argentina, Chile and Peru.
At its centre stands the equestrian monument dedicated to San Martín and the armies of independence. The square was named in his honour in 1878, on the centenary of his birth, and subsequently developed into one of Buenos Aires' principal public spaces.
The Pope's arrival in Argentina marks the second stage of his 12-day, three-country apostolic journey, which began in Uruguay and will conclude in Peru on 16 November.

articles.title_orig: Saudi Arabia intercepts missiles as Aramco building in Riyadh is damaged, and other Mideast news
articles.title_zh: Saudi Arabia intercepts missiles as Aramco building in Riyadh is damaged, and other Mideast news
articles.content_orig:
Egypt, Bahrain, Kuwait and Syria have condemned the latest Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia , after an attempted strike damaged an administrative building belonging to state oil giant Saudi Aramco in Riyadh.
Saudi authorities said air defence systems intercepted several missiles on Sunday, November 8, 2026, as security warnings spread across parts of the kingdom's oil-rich Eastern Province.
Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Energy confirmed that falling debris damaged an administrative building of Saudi Aramco, the kingdom’s $1.7 trillion state-owned oil giant, in Riyadh’s King Abdullah Financial District, but no casualties were reported.
Houthi military spokesperson Brigadier General Yahya Saree claimed responsibility for the operation, saying the group had targeted Riyadh's financial district in response to Saudi attacks in Yemen.
According to Saree, strikes on a village near Sanaa and a market in southwestern Yemen had left dozens dead or injured. His casualty claims could not be independently verified.
DON'T MISS: Middle East’s largest Arab economy says it has provided $145 billion in global aid, with India, Egypt, Nigeria and Yemen among beneficiaries
In response, Egypt's Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the attacks as a "flagrant violation of international law" and Saudi Arabia's sovereignty, warning that they posed "a direct threat to civilians".
Cairo also expressed solidarity with Riyadh and backed measures taken by the kingdom to protect its territory and citizens.
Egypt's position comes weeks after its parliament approved President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi's request to provide defensive military assistance to Saudi Arabia if needed.
Lawmakers granted the authorisation on October 26, although Cairo has not announced any deployment of troops to the kingdom.
Bahrain, an oil-rich Gulf state, also condemned the attacks, reaffirming Saudi Arabia's right to self-defence under Article 51 of the United Nations Charter and urging the UN Security Council to address repeated strikes on the kingdom.
Fellow oil-rich Gulf nation Kuwait denounced the missile and drone attacks, warning that they endangered civilian lives and threatened regional stability.
Syria, for its part, condemned the targeting of Riyadh's financial district and the Aramco facility, expressing support for Saudi Arabia's sovereignty and security.
DON'T MISS: Like Canada, Africa’s largest car producer faces 2027 job and export losses as world’s $32 trillion economy ends duty-free access, with China and Europe offering hope
Earlier on Sunday, Saudi Civil Defence issued security alerts in several areas of the Eastern Province, including Dhahran, where Aramco has its headquarters, before lifting the warnings.
The province holds most of Saudi Arabia's oil and gas reserves. Aramco's headquarters in Dhahran had already suffered extensive damage in a separate attack in October.
Saudi coalition forces also reported intercepting a ballistic missile aimed at the kingdom's southern region, near the Yemeni border.
Sunday's attacks followed an October 10 strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport that killed 13 people and injured more than 300, according to Saudi authorities, further disrupting the relative calm established by a UN-brokered truce in 2022.
Saudi Arabia entered Yemen's civil war in 2015 to restore the internationally recognised government after the Houthis seized Sanaa, beginning years of conflict that have caused a humanitarian crisis and exposed Saudi infrastructure to repeated missile and drone attacks.

articles.title_orig: Chinese carmaker BYD’s offices in Netherlands raided over JLR ‘copycat car’ claim
articles.title_zh: Chinese carmaker BYD’s offices in Netherlands raided over JLR ‘copycat car’ claim
articles.content_orig:
Bailiffs reportedly seized digital records before court case over alleged intellectual property breaches on Land Rover Defender
Bailiffs acting for Jaguar Land Rover raided the Dutch offices of a Chinese “copycat” rival before a legal showdown this week over whether its “Defender clone” infringes intellectual property rights.
Bailiffs acting on behalf of JLR reportedly seized digital records from the offices of Chinese carmaker BYD in Schiedam and Hoofddorp in August, according to the Sunday Times.
The raid took place before a court case in the The Hague this week which will decide whether the BYD has a case to answer over allegations that its Ti7 SUV infringes the intellectual property of the Land Rover Defender.
Motoring experts have likened BYD’s seven-seat plug-in hybrid SUV to the Defender since it went on sale in China in September last year. The company is scheduled to launch the vehicle, which the BBC’s Top Gear magazine called the “Chinese Defender clone” , in the UK market in January at a price of £47,995, undercutting the Defender by more than £20,000.
BYD says on its website that “an unapologetically boxy profile delivers the imposing, chunky design that finds favour among SUV buyers, yet delivers a contemporary look”.
The price of JLR’s seven-seat Defender 110 starts from £68,465and is one of the country’s bestselling cars. The UK-based carmaker, which is owned by India’s Tata Motors, sold 29,500 Defenders to retail customers between July and September this year, compared with 25,370a year earlier.
The raid in the Netherlands was carried out by court-ordered bailiffs, with JLR suspecting that BYD reverse-engineered some of the technology that could be used in the Ti7, the Times reported. JLR wanted to secure the digital records before they could be destroyed.
JLR and BYD declined to comment on the “ongoing legal proceedings”.
The dispute with BYD is not the first legal case JLR has pursed against a Chinese company over copycat allegations. It won a legal case to stop Jiangling Motor Corporation selling a copycat vehicle in 2019 after a three-year court battle.

In some cases JLR has taken a collaborative approach to dealing with the rise of China’s carmakers. It agreed to form a joint venture with Chery in a 2012 deal which later included licensing its discontinued Freelander brand with the company.
Chery’s Jaecoo model, which is not part of the joint venture, has been called the Temu Range Rover because of its similarities to the JLR vehicle after years of collaboration between the pair. It costs £10,000 less than JLR’s Range Rover.
The Jaecoo was the bestselling car in the UK in October, with 10,813 registrations, taking its market share from 2.07% to 4.30%, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers & Traders. JLR’s sales of the Range Rover fell to 43,300 in the third quarter of this year, from 47,196 cars sold in the same months last year.

articles.title_orig: Hundreds of thousands join Amsterdam’s ‘Red Line’ protest against Israel
articles.title_zh: Hundreds of thousands join Amsterdam’s ‘Red Line’ protest against Israel
articles.content_orig:
More than 200,000 people have taken to the streets of Amsterdam in the Netherlands, demanding government action against Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, according to the Dutch branch of Amnesty International, one of the organisers.
Sunday’s ‘Red Line’ protesters, many wearing red items of clothing, called for tighter trade restrictions on Israel and a halt to all arms sales.
“What is happening there is inhumane,” Mike van Dongen said as he walked in the huge throng of people.
“As far as I’m concerned, [the Dutch authorities] are doing nothing,” he said. “They don’t dare take any serious steps.”
As the protesters marched along a normally busy Amsterdam street that was closed to traffic on Sunday, a man stood at a bus stop with a loudspeaker shouting, “Free, free Palestine!” Many of the marchers echoed his cry as they passed.
Israel’s genocidal war has killed at least 74,000 Palestinians, including 21,000 children, since October 2023.
Sunday’s protest was similar to one in early October last year. That followed ‘Red Line’ demonstrations last June when protesters marched through the streets of The Hague.
A “ ceasefire ” took effect in Gaza on October 10 last year, but Israeli attacks and killings have continued on an almost-daily basis since.
The war in Gaza has strained relations between the Netherlands and Israel. The Dutch foreign minister resigned last year after failing to secure new sanctions against Israel.
Since then, a new minority coalition government took power in February and introduced an import ban on products from Israeli settlements, which the Dutch government and most of the international community consider illegal – the ban provoked a diplomatic spat with Israel.
Prime Minister Rob Jetten, who took part in a march last year but was not present on Sunday, defended his government’s actions at his weekly news conference on Friday.
“Every single day and every single week, we do what we can to alleviate the terrible situation there,” he said.
He added that his administration is “exerting greater political and diplomatic pressure” on Israel to abide by its agreements on Gaza.

Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility , your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility !
Almost seven years ago, while clutching a laptop, my phone, and a notebook in a sea of Tesla fans, I watched head designer Franz von Holzhausen throw a metal, baseball-sized ball at the driver’s-side window of the Cybertruck . The result was cracked glass — actually, two by the end of the presentation — and some awkward jokes and chuckling by CEO Elon Musk .
I have witnessed a number of stunning, odd, and fantastical moments at Tesla events. But the Cybertruck reveal was the most interesting — and not because of the postapocalyptic design. It was the crowd.
When the truck rolled out onto the stage, I watched attendees gasp, some in revulsion. There was mumbling (“This certainly can’t be the Cybertruck ?” I heard Tesla superfans whisper). And yes, there were cheers. The momentary shock of Musk’s biggest fans was quickly replaced by support, acceptance, and finally, endorsement.
It moved like a wave over the crowd. By the time attendees were waiting in line for Cybertruck rides, the mood had shifted. Everyone was a fan.
That fandom carried over to Cybertruck reservations, which skyrocketed to 1 million, Musk said during a third-quarter earnings call in 2023. But it never made the leap to actual sales. Industry experts estimate about 71,000 Cybertrucks have been sold since the first deliveries began in November 2023.
And now the Cybertruck is headed to the scrap pile. Tesla will stop making the Cybertruck next year, Musk said Friday.
Was the vehicle too edgy? Maybe, but this was always going to be a niche market. I believe more practical reasons dampened sales. Musk promised the Cybertruck would have a 500-mile range and a price tag under $40,000. It achieved neither, senior reporter Sean O’Kane noted in his report .
Zipline has had quite the week. Strike that — quite the year. The autonomous drone delivery startup, which was founded in 2014, has steadily scaled over the past few years. But 2026 has taken the company to new heights.
In early 2026, Zipline raised $600 million and quickly added another $200 million to that Series H round. The company planned to use these funds to accelerate its expansion to at least four U.S. cities in 2026.
Now it has even more money to grow even faster. Zipline announced this week it raised $1.5 billion and ramped up its partnership with Walmart to add 300 drone delivery sites across the United States. Zipline is now valued at $21.5 billion.
Other deals that got my attention …
Electric truck startup Harbinger raised a $240 million Series D funding round as it expands its portfolio of products, including battery storage and defense applications. No word on the company’s valuation.
Humble Robotics raised $51 million in a Series A round, bringing total funding to $75 million less than a year after founding. The round was led by Obvious Ventures with participation from insiders Eclipse, Energy Impact Partners, and others.
Static Media acquired automotive news site CarScoops, adding to its existing portfolio that includes 34 brands such as Engadget, Jalopnik, and SlashGear.
Also , the micromobility startup spun out of Rivian in 2025, quietly started and then walked away from an electric two-wheeler pilot project in Kenya earlier this year, as it sought to focus its resources on its consumer e-bike and autonomous vehicle ambitions.
Amazon has made Uber Eats its official restaurant delivery partner for Prime members in the United States, effectively ending the e-commerce giant’s existing deal with Grubhub.
The Luce, Ferrari ’s first electric car and one of its most polarizing models, is “fully allocated” for 2027.
Ford unveiled what it’s calling a “privacy promise” — an “explicit commitment” to keep customers’ vehicle data safe and give them control over what they share. Ford also launched a website designed to educate customers about how, where, and why the automaker uses their data, and to show them how to change those settings.
May Mobility and Forterra advanced to phase three of the Department of Defense’s Robotic Operations for Autonomous Delivery and Sustainment (ROADS) prize challenge, an initiative to test and adopt commercial self-driving vehicles in the military.
Serve Robotics announced plans to launch a new business line called Physical AI Services. The company will still operate and expand its autonomous delivery operations and become a technology supplier to other companies building robots.
The predictions of AI agents booking restaurants, trips, and even rides for the masses hasn’t quite materialized yet. Uber reported during its third-quarter earnings call that only four rides were ordered through an AI agent during its busiest week in October: the week of Halloween.
Waymo is shaking up its Uber relationship, confirming months of speculation. The company will end its exclusivity with Uber in the Austin and Atlanta markets starting in January 2028.
Over the past three years, this newsletter often highlighted an investigation, scoop, or interview from senior reporter Sean O’Kane . Some of my favorites were the articles we collaborated on, including his scoop that Jeff Bezos was backing Slate Auto , our story about how Jony Ive’s LoveFrom had worked on the design of the Also e-bike , his investigation into Fisker, and his coverage of how Waymo was relying on first responders to help move its robotaxis.
We have co-bylined dozens of articles on company earnings and breaking news and co-hosted Equity, TechCrunch’s flagship podcast about the business of startups. And so it’s bittersweet to see him head off on a new adventure at the Wall Street Journal to cover Tesla.
Congrats on the gig, Sean! We hate to see you go!
I will, of course, continue to deliver readers insider details, scoops, and analysis about the future of transportation, from autonomous vehicle technology and EVs to automotive tech and the future of flight.

articles.title_orig: Seven dead and more than 100 injured after trains collide in Egypt
articles.title_zh: Seven dead and more than 100 injured after trains collide in Egypt
articles.content_orig:
Footage shows derailed train carriages near Giza in Egypt
At least seven people have died in a train crash near the Egyptian city of Giza, with more than 100 injured.
The country's railway authority said two trains travelling south from Giza and Cairo collided, causing several carriages to derail and fall down an embankment.
Images from the scene showed people looking inside overturned carriages for injured passengers as a massive emergency response was launched.
Egyptian President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi said he had ordered state authorities to "investigate the circumstances of the accident, and hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent".
The public prosecutor's office warned the death toll could rise.
Uninjured passengers and passersby searched derailed carriages for injured people
The government said hospitals in the area had been put "on heightened alert" as they dealt with a massive influx of patients.
Egypt's health minister Dr Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said people were being treated for broken bones and head injuries.
The driver of one of the trains was among those who died in the crash, the ministry confirmed.
The first train involved in the crash was travelling from Giza to Fayoum, south of Cairo, when it crashed into the rear of another service heading south from Cairo to Aswan, which was stationary on the tracks.
Images from the scene showed some carriages had overturned, with the body of at least one appearing to have split in two.
Trains between Giza and the Upper Egypt region were suspended as cranes were dispatched to remove the wrecked trains.
The collision occurred in the area between Kafr Ammar and Al-Raqqa stations in Al-Ayyat, close to where Egypt's deadliest train tragedy occurred in February 2002, when a fire engulfed a passenger train travelling from Cairo to Luxor.
The train continued for around nine kilometres (5.6 miles) before coming to a halt.
In that incident, more than 370 people were officially reported killed, although some estimates put the toll considerably higher.
Two further crashes in the area in 2009 killed dozens more.
There were calls in Egypt on Sunday for the transport minister to resign over the latest deadly rail disaster.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang reportedly targeted by Beijing-recruited spy
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang reportedly targeted by Beijing-recruited spy
articles.content_orig:
Lawmakers from both sides of the aisle are ramping up calls for investigations into reports of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. Some are also questioning what the Trump administration knew about the matter.
"The more I learn about the insane relationship between the Trump Administration, Chinese spies, and AI billionaires, the more I'm convinced there is nothing this administration does that isn't corrupt," Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., posted on X on Saturday. "Congress will investigate and get answers."
Coons is in line to chair the Senate Foreign Relations Committee when his party takes control of the chamber in January.
Three House Republican committee chairs sent a letter to Huang on Wednesday requesting that he sit for a closed-door briefing with lawmakers on Nov. 18, a day after the company is scheduled to report third-quarter earnings.
"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the [People's Republic of China's] access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," the GOP lawmakers wrote in a letter to Huang .
The reports refer to Huang's alleged relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based tech company that the U.S. has suspected of helping China circumvent artificial intelligence chip sales prohibitions.
Policymakers in the Trump administration received a memo last spring with intelligence identifying Alice Huang as having been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security and revealing her relationship with Nvidia's chief executive, The New York Times first reported on Friday.
When asked by the Times whether Huang would appear before lawmakers to discuss the matter, Nvidia spokesman John Rizzo declined to comment. "Our chief executive has an outstanding security team that accompanies him where needed," Mr. Rizzo said in a statement to the Times.
Rizzo said the Nvidia CEO's interactions with Ms. Huang were consistent with meetings he has had with any of Nvidia's customers, the Times reported .
Separately, Texas Republican Sen. John Cornyn shared a Times article published Saturday reporting that the Trump administration approved a Chinese firm, New Matrix, to assemble chips for Nvidia in Beijing. The Times found little evidence of meaningful operations at its listed address, despite Trump's Commerce Department clearing it for national security risks.
Cornyn called the report "outrageous" in his post on X .
Rep. Seth Magaziner, D-R.I., who sits on the House Committee on Homeland Security, called on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify before Congress along with Huang.
Neither Nvidia nor the Commerce Department immediately responded to CNBC's request for comment.

articles.title_orig: Rosstat hack: data obtained suggests over 390,000 Russian deaths in Ukraine war
articles.title_zh: Rosstat hack: data obtained suggests over 390,000 Russian deaths in Ukraine war
articles.content_orig:
The hacker groups Kiberpartizany BY and Silent Crow claim to have carried out a large-scale breach of Russia's Federal State Statistics Service (Rosstat).
According to the hackers, they managed to steal about 23 terabytes of data, including internal documents, demographic and economic statistics, as well as information on Russian losses in the war against Ukraine.
The data obtained enabled the groups to make their own calculations of the number of people killed since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
According to Kiberpartizany BY, as of 27 August 2026 at least 393,881 Russian citizens have been killed in the war. Silent Crow gives an even higher figure of 450,100 dead.
This significant difference in estimates is due to the use of different methods of counting losses.
Kiberpartizany BY counted deaths in which military action or its consequences were listed as the cause.
Silent Crow, by contrast, not only included those killed in combat, but also added several other categories of deaths: non-combat losses among military personnel, deaths marked as terrorist acts, and deaths of people registered in Russia but who died in occupied territories or in Ukraine where the exact cause of death was not established.
Russia has not released official statistics on combat losses since September 2022.
In addition, from 2024 Rosstat stopped publishing annual data on causes of death, which has made an independent assessment of the demographic impact of the war much more difficult.
Against this backdrop, access to the agency's internal statistical materials may make it possible to assess the scale of human losses more accurately.
For comparison, as of 8 November the joint database of BBC News Russian Service and Mediazona, which collects a list of dead Russian servicemen identified by name, contained around 286,000 names. However, this list is known to be incomplete, especially for the most recent months of the war.
In a joint study by Meduza and Mediazona, based on analysis of inheritance registry data, the number of fallen Russian servicemen by the end of 2025 was estimated at roughly 350,000.
In this way, the hackers' estimates are in line with figures from previously published independent studies, although this does not yet prove the accuracy of each individual number.
Meduza and Mediazona have said they obtained access to the data published by the hackers and have begun checking it.
The journalists aim to establish not only whether the materials are authentic, but also how complete the information is they contain. In particular, they need to rule out the possibility of deliberate data falsification.
Moreover, causes of death given in medical documents do not always reflect the actual circumstances of a person's death.
It should also be noted that Rosstat's internal databases do not contain up-to-date information on people listed as missing. Such individuals may be declared dead only after a long period of time.
Therefore even data from the state statistics agency cannot automatically provide a definitive figure for Russian military losses.
If the authenticity and completeness of the leak are confirmed, the materials obtained could become one of the largest sources of information on the demographic consequences of the war for Russia.

articles.title_orig: South Africa’s ANC is humbled by its worst election results
articles.title_zh: South Africa’s ANC is humbled by its worst election results
articles.content_orig:
South Africa's ANC has recorded its worst-ever showing in local elections since Nelson Mandela led the country out of apartheid and into democracy more than 30 years ago, a result the party has called "catastrophic".
While it won the most votes of all parties in the country, the African National Congress won 30.76% of the overall vote, one third down from the 46% it gained in 2021, and a far cry from the 64.82% 20 years ago.
The story of its decline is also clear in the provinces and cities. The party won a majority in just one of the country's nine provinces, Limpopo. In 2021 it won six. It also won the most votes in just two of the eight cities, compared with six at the last local elections.
The Democratic Alliance (DA) came second in the overall vote with 24.64%, retaining majority control of the city of Cape Town. Former president Jacob Zuma's MK party came third overall with 9.76%, unseating the ANC as winner in the city of Durban, while the Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF), led by Julius Malema, once seen as a serious challenge to the ANC, came fourth with 6.22%.
"This has been a very catastrophic outcome for the ANC," said secretary-general Fikile Mbalula on Saturday. "We knew this disaster is coming, we're staring at it. As we got into elections, the cost of living of our people was too high. The middle class have turned on the ANC in big numbers."
Entering the count centre tonight, South Africa's president and leader of the ANC Cyril Ramaphosa said: "We accept the will of the people however concerning it might be, we accept that this is how the people of South Africa in our towns, in our cities, in our metros have spoken - and this is their verdict, we accept it with humility. It is a decline that is concerning, that is how I characterise it."
It's a continuing decline for the ANC, which lost majority rule in the national elections in 2024 for the first time in its history. It then had to form a coalition government with a raft of other parties in what is now known as the GNU, or government of national unity.
While the Democratic Alliance made significant gains in the cities in these local elections, its overall vote share rose marginally from 21.83% in 2021, and was below the 26.9% it gained in 2016.
Voter turnout was 52.29%, an increase from 45.9% in 2021, when elections were held during the Covid pandemic.
"This election is delivering a devastating message to the ANC", said political analyst Susan Booysen. "It's an ANC in decline at local municipal level, at the metropolitan level, and when the results are reflected provincially and nationally, we see severe declines in ANC levels of support all around."
The reason for that decline in support is largely due to poor service delivery and infrastructure across the country, from water and power to sanitation. "These are huge problems," says Booysen, "and have really been affecting the lives of ordinary people, in the suburbs, in the townships, and in very dramatic ways."
The big picture looks even more bleak for the ANC. The party will elect a new leader next year as Cyril Ramaphosa comes to end of his term. He is due to stay on as president of the country until the next national elections in 2029, but there are few candidates lined up to succeed him in either role.
"It is sort of the end of the liberation movement era in South Africa," said political analyst William Gumede, "and the dominance of the liberation movement since the end of apartheid. So the ANC is going to be a party that by 2029 could be the second biggest rather than the biggest party. It may actually spiral into a long period of just total infighting. This is a new era for South Africa's politics and also the ANC."
The elections also saw a significant shift in voting patterns, with the DA, traditionally known as the "white party" for attracting a largely white vote, gaining more black votes. "We're moving towards a post-racial voting pattern in South Africa," added Gumede.
South Africa now faces days of local coalition building, with the three metropolitan municipalities in the province of Gauteng, the country's powerhouse, under particular scrutiny. The ANC may even find itself shut out in the cities of Johannesburg and Pretoria.
"We are now in a coalition country," said Gumede. "Essentially, what the voters are saying is, "Well, the ANC has dominated the last three decades, they didn't use their power to change the society for the good, so we don't want the dominant parties anymore, whether at national level, provincial level, or rather now at a local level. We actually want coalitions. We want people to work together."
Parties now have 14 days from the moment results were announced to negotiate coalitions.

articles.title_orig: 2 big AI narratives wrestle with each other: What to watch this week
articles.title_zh: 2 big AI narratives wrestle with each other: What to watch this week
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Even before the sell-off last week, we've all had the feeling of white-knuckling through the fourth quarter.
Anthropic's ( ANTH.PVT ) IPO prospectus. Big Tech earnings. Bond yields through the roof. An unexpectedly tall blue wave that lifted the stock market up — and threw it back down.
With volatility ( ^VIX ) running hot, investors are balancing on a knife's edge between a flywheel of angst — or a bounce.
As Goldman Sachs' panic gauge suggested, the extremeness may signal more of Friday's bounce to come.
It's a new week, and we'll have plenty of scheduled plot points to guide us.
Of particular note, we're looking forward to CoreWeave ( CRWV ) quarterly results on Tuesday and Nebius Group ( NBIS ) and Cerebras Systems ( CBRS ) on Thursday, a few companies caught up in the data center destruction post-election.
What they have to say about their plans and outlook, the debt markets they've been tapping, and the health of their business will be at the top of mind.
Good timing to have that a mere week after midterms.
On the economic calendar, we're in inflation mode once again, especially after that hot jobs report.
We'll kick off the week with the New York Fed's consumer inflation expectations before getting some actual data on Tuesday — and wholesale inflation figures on Friday to close the week.
What's more important: the chip and AI infrastructure trade or the companies that actually provide AI?
As we wrote in the Morning Brief on Friday, "A data center slowdown is bad for the stock market's AI engine," and "A data center slowdown is good for Big Tech's profit machine."
Can Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ), Microsoft ( MSFT ), and Amazon ( AMZN ) deliver AI at least some productivity and tools to clients with the compute they have — and make a lot of money doing so, flipping the switch from growth and scale to monetization?
Maybe! Those companies are healthily in the green since the election, doing just fine amid the broader sell-off. And while Tesla ( TSLA ) has sold off, SpaceX ( SPCX ) is mostly doing fine.
As DataTrek's Nicholas Colas wrote on Thursday, you need to look at the entire week, not just the bloody Thursday, to see the bigger picture (small as that is). And it's pretty clear that this may be reflected in the broad indexes, but it's mostly about chips.
"As for what the market is 'saying' over the last 2 days, we believe the moves are AI-centric, not augurs of a looming recession," Colas wrote, also noting that Google and Co. are doing fine.
The push-pull of the chip narrative and the hyperscaler narrative is the pulse our fingers are on right now.
Friday's blowout jobs report of 165,000 jobs delivered an unexpected verdict about the current state of the labor market: It's better than fine.
Even September's underwhelming 29,000 jobs were adjusted upward to 60,000.
Good for breaking the "low-fire, low-hire" ice, if this represents the beginning of a trend. As every Fed chair likes to remind us, one month doesn't mean anything by itself.
The big takeaway from the report, however, isn't that the labor market is heating up, but that any weakness or recession is not currently something to worry about .
But with Tuesday and Friday's big inflation reports for October, we'll have more than just one data point to work with, and two (or more) hot pieces of economic data could start to make some people sweat.
We are keeping one research note from Apollo's Torsten Sløk that caught our attention last week at the top of our mind: that the Fed's rates needed to bring inflation down its 2% target could be as high as 6.75%. (Disclosure: Yahoo is a portfolio company of funds managed by affiliates of Apollo Global Management.)
While the data center sell-off is obviously important, inflation still matters as much as anything.
Bloomberg's average analyst estimate has core inflation rising 0.2%, slowing down from 0.3% last month.
Amid all the data will be a lot of commentary from the people who read the data — and decide what to do with it.
The Fed's Goolsbee and Bowman speak on Monday; Waller and Bowman (again) on Tuesday; Barr, Barkin, and Logan on Thursday; and Williams, Jefferson, and Bowman (again) on Friday.
We love seeing our public officials putting in the work. But the market loves guidance and FedSpeak even more and is hoping to be given more of a lens through which to read all of this data and get a better picture of how the Fed sees the economy — and perhaps even the sell-off, depending on what topics come up and how forthcoming they feel like being.
Right now, after Friday's jobs report, the December hike is feeling more likely.
With Fed Chair Warsh settling into a cryptic, taciturn no-forward-guidance rhythm, it's up to these guys — who may also feel more emboldened post-midterms.
As JPMorgan noted last week , the new Democratic Senate leadership is going to be important for the Fed.

articles.title_orig: Nasa seeks next generation of astronauts to live and work on the moon
articles.title_zh: Nasa seeks next generation of astronauts to live and work on the moon
articles.content_orig:
Applications due on 3 December for new generation of explorers who can ‘shape humanity’s future in space’
Nasa has launched a callout for a new generation of astronauts as it searches for explorers who could live and work on the moon.
Opening applications for the latest expansion of its Artemis program , the US agency said successful candidates would help “shape humanity’s future in space” as it builds a base on the moon and plans the first crewed missions to Mars.
The news was announced on Saturday during a Kennedy Space Center air show promoting lunar exploration, as well as advances in aviation and technology.
“This is an extraordinary time to join Nasa’s astronaut corps,” said Nasa administrator Jared Isaacman. “The people we select could walk on the Moon, live and work at the Moon Base, and help pioneer the systems and operations that will ultimately carry crews to Mars.”
Nasa expects to make its final selection in late 2027 to begin training the next class of astronaut candidates. The agency last opened applications for new astronauts in 2024, ultimately accepting 10 new astronauts out of more than 8,000 applicants in September 2025.
“For those who apply, becoming a Nasa astronaut is more than a career opportunity,” said Scott Tingle, chief astronaut and chair of the Astronaut Selection Board at Nasa’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. “It is a chance to join a legacy of explorers who have pushed the boundaries of discovery and play a role in the missions that will shape humanity’s future in space.”
Since the 1960s, Nasa has selected 370 people to train as astronaut candidates for increasingly challenging missions. The agency currently has 32 astronauts active in the astronaut corps.
Isaacman and other agency leaders recently laid out Nasa’s ambitions to return Americans to the moon in 2028. Both SpaceX and Blue Origin intend to support a crewed lunar landing.
All applicants must be US citizens, Nasa said, and have either a master’s degree in science, technology, engineering or mathematics; medical qualifications; training as a pilot; or two years’ work on a relevant doctoral program.
Three years of “related professional experience” are also required.
Applying pilots must have either 750 hours of pilot-in-command time of a high-performance jet, 1,500 total flight hours in another fixed-wing aircraft, or 1,000 total flight hours in a rotary-wing aircraft.
Applicants have until 11.59pm ET on Thursday, 3 December, to submit their applications.
